title: Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness
research_question: This study compares the biological effects of reading an electronic book on a light-emitting device (LE-eBook) with reading a printed book in the hours before bedtime, examining impacts on sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness.

participants.description: Twelve healthy young adults (mean ± SD: 24.92 ± 2.87 y; six women) from Boston, MA, USA.
participants.recruitment: Informed written consent was obtained. Participants were compensated for their participation and extensively screened for physical and psychological health, excluding those with chronic conditions, sleep disorders, or recent shift work/travel. They maintained a fixed 8-h sleep schedule (10:00 PM to 6:00 AM) for 3 weeks prior to admission.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Reading an electronic book on a light-emitting device (LE-eBook, iPad; Apple Inc.) set to maximum brightness, held at a fixed distance (30-45 cm) from the eye, in very dim room light (~3 lx) for ~4 h before bedtime for five consecutive evenings.

Reading a printed book by reflected light, held at a desired distance from the eye, in the same very dim room light (~3 lx) for ~4 h before bedtime for five consecutive evenings. Participants supplied their own books.

mechanisms: Acute alerting effect of light from light-emitting eReaders (LE-eBooks) in the evening.
Delay of the circadian timing system due to evening light exposure from LE-eBooks.
Suppression of melatonin secretion by evening light exposure from LE-eBooks.
Differences in the prior sleep episode (e.g., reduced REM sleep) contributing to next-morning sleepiness.
Short-wavelength-enriched light emitted by LE-eBooks causing greater melatonin suppression and phase-shifting responses.
implementation_implications: The use of light-emitting devices immediately before bedtime increases alertness, which may lead users to delay bedtime at home.
The biological effects of portable light-emitting devices used before bedtime may perpetuate sleep deficiency and disrupt circadian rhythms, potentially impacting performance, health, and safety.

Further investigation into the physiological and medical effects of electronic devices is warranted due to potential longer-term health consequences of acute responses to short-wavelength-enriched light.
Physiological studies on the impact of such light exposure on children and adolescents, particularly concerning learning and development, are needed.

tables.description: Photopic illuminance and human retinal photopigment-weighted illuminance measures from the LE-eBook device and light reflected by the printed book.

limitations: Melatonin suppression was assessed only on the fifth and final evening of each reading condition, potentially missing earlier effects.
The evening reading sessions were 4 hours long, which may not reflect typical usage patterns for all users.
The LE-eBook was set to maximum brightness throughout the reading session, which may not be representative of all user habits.
The LE-eBook reader was held at a fixed distance (30-45 cm) from the eye, which is further than many users might hold smaller devices, potentially reducing retinal light exposure.

The study did not include a light-emitting device with longer wavelength for comparison, making it difficult to definitively attribute findings to short-wavelength light versus overall irradiance level.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: SignificanceThe use of light-emitting electronic devices for reading, communication, and entertainment has greatly increased recently. We found that the use of these devices before bedtime prolongs the time it takes to fall asleep, delays the circadian clock, suppresses levels of the sleep-promoting hormone melatonin, reduces the amount and delays the timing of REM sleep, and reduces alertness the following morning. Use of light-emitting devices immediately before bedtime also increases alertness at that time, which may lead users to delay bedtime at home. Overall, we found that the use of portable light-emitting devices immediately before bedtime has biological effects that may perpetuate sleep deficiency and disrupt circadian rhythms, both of which can have adverse impacts on performance, health, and safety.

mechanism_chain.description: Light emitted from eReaders, particularly in the blue spectrum, activates retinal photoreceptors, signaling to the brain's circadian clock (SCN), which suppresses melatonin production and shifts circadian timing, leading to disrupted sleep and reduced next-morning alertness.

steps.to_construct: Activation of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)
Signal transmission to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)
Suppression of melatonin production from the pineal gland

steps.from_construct: Melatonin suppression and circadian phase shift
steps.to_construct: Disrupted sleep and reduced next-morning alertness

instruments_used.name: Salivary Melatonin Assay
instruments_used.description: Measurement of melatonin concentration in saliva samples to assess circadian timing and light-induced suppression.

instruments_used.name: Polysomnography (PSG)
instruments_used.construct: Sleep architecture (e.g., sleep latency, REM latency, sleep efficiency, sleep stages)
instruments_used.description: Simultaneous recording of electroencephalogram (EEG), electrooculogram (EOG), and electromyogram (EMG) to objectively assess sleep parameters.

instruments_used.name: Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS)
instruments_used.description: A 9-point self-report scale used to assess current levels of sleepiness.

instruments_used.name: Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT)
instruments_used.description: A simple reaction time task used to measure sustained attention and vigilance, often used to assess the impact of sleep deprivation.

instruments_used.name: Spectroradiometer
instruments_used.description: Device used to characterize the spectral power distribution and intensity of light emitted by eReaders and ambient light conditions.
